en: The śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.
Next, as for the characteristics of the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), it is stated: the following clarifies the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
As for the aforementioned path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it exists only in the initial mind of entering the first bhūmi; now, this path of cultivation excludes [that].
From the initial entry into the mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*),
through the completion of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and abiding in the mind that emerges from the stage,
up until the diamond-like uninterrupted path (*vajrānantaryamārga*) at the end of the tenth stage.
This is also called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Having raised this question,
it shall be understood in detail below.
Treatise.
The verse says: "Upon arrival, one immediately realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The commentary says:
This is answered by citing a verse:
"From the moment of emerging from the mind abiding in the first bhūmi,
one gradually proceeds until reaching the ultimate Vajra Path."
Because they have severed all seeds of innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
they realize the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Treatise.
"From the bodhisattva up to non-conceptual wisdom.
Commentary: The subsequent explanation has two parts.
First, there is a brief explanation of the verses;
second, an extensive explanation of the meaning of the verses.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, an explanation of the initial three lines which directly reveal the characteristics of the stages.
It is explained later that at this stage of cultivation, one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) upon reaching the ultimate stage.

One cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) during the path of cultivation of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in order to sever remaining obstacles and realize the transformation of the basis, and so forth.
This introduces the following passage:
However, it is not that wisdom alone constitutes the essence of the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).
Here, we speak briefly of the path capable of severing [afflictions] by way of its object of focus (*ālambana*), and do not mention the others.
Treatise:
This wisdom is remote and inconceivable.
Commentary: It is said:
To be far removed from the grasped object (*grāhya*) is called "non-attainment" (*anupalabdhi*);
to be far removed from the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) is said to be "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

This explains the first line of the verse above: that is, the single essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*), being free from the conceptualization of a real grasped object and a grasping subject as they are falsely imagined (*parikalpita*), is described as "non-attainment" and so forth.
It is not that the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth do not exist. According to the treatise,
it is called "inconceivable" because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The commentary states:
The essence of this single wisdom is devoid of conceptual discrimination;
that which possesses conceptual discrimination is a mode of activity characterized by frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is also termed conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Alternatively, tainted conceptualization (*sāsrava-vikalpa*) is designated as conceptual proliferation because it increases biased attachment; therefore, it is called conceptual proliferation.
Thus, subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) is not termed conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
According to the former interpretation,
non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), which is capable of severing the two obscurations, is termed "sublime function."
This is inconceivable.
If one relies on the latter interpretation,
then all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is free from faults.
The ability to transcend birth and death is called "wondrous function," which is inconceivable.
In this present passage, however, we rely solely on the former interpretation,
as the treatise itself makes it clear.
Treatise:
This is supramundane, reaching non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Commentary states:
Explaining the second line of the verse:
non-conceptual wisdom is interpreted as possessing two meanings,
namely, the severance of the mundane world.
Its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth;
the subsequently attained [wisdom] is not thus,
and is therefore not called supramundane (*lokottara*).
Treatise:
Because one practices this repeatedly, it is therefore called "equanimity" (upekṣā). Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Explaining the third line of the verse:
that which opposes the subtle is called coarse;
that which opposes the light is called heavy.
The seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) termed "heavy impediments" (*dausthulya*),
as well as those heavy impediments that are not seeds, are abandoned stage by stage.
The seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) termed "heavy impediments" [are likewise abandoned].
The *vajra* [samādhi] first eliminates them;
as for the afflictions that are not of the nature of seeds but are coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
these are also abandoned stage by stage.
This now clarifies that by cultivating non-conceptual wisdom through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
one severs the seeds of afflictions at the diamond-like mind (*vajramānas*),
while severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and so forth throughout the ten stages and other levels.
Taken collectively, these are termed the "abandonment of two kinds.
In terms of ultimate exhaustion, this occurs solely at the stage of the vajra-like [samādhi].
At the moment the vajra is exhausted, one realizes the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Treatise:
This ability to relinquish that leads to the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Commentary:
Because the cultivation of wisdom through the ten stages reaches its consummation,
one attains the Buddha’s realization of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
This explains the fourth line of the verse.
Within this, there are two successive expositions;
these constitute the two parts.
Treatise:
"Reliance" refers to the reliance upon the two fruits of transformation.
[The commentary] states:
This is now the first interpretation.
In summary, because the general serves as the basis for severing the specific defilements, there is no clinging;
because it gives rise to purity, one attains the two fruits.
The remaining text is easy to understand.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as the abandonment of results;
the ninth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s commentary (*Vasubandhu-ṭīkā*) treats it similarly.
That passage is somewhat more extensive: "As for what is called the transformation of the basis..."
"Transformation" (parāvṛtti) refers to the relinquishing of one state and the acquisition of another.
"Basis" (āśraya) refers to that which serves as the support.
Thus, the basis of transformation is termed the "transformation of the basis" (āśrayaparāvṛtti).

The Tatpuruṣa (dependent) explanation: Furthermore, this text is interpreted as follows: regarding the phenomena of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), there is the clinging to false principles and the detachment from correct principles through the reversal of error.
Because these phenomena serve as the basis for the principles, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Wu-xing says:
"The two bases; 'transformation of the basis' (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is also explained by way of a karmadhāraya compound."
However, since the supported (āśrita) and the support (āśraya) are now combined to form the "transformation of the basis" (āśrayaparāvṛtti),
there is no case of a genitive compound (tatpuruṣa). Thus,
when it is said that "the dependent nature arises as the transformation of the basis," [it refers to this].
It is the basis for transmigration and cessation;
that is, what is abandoned and what is attained.
What is attained pertains to both types of fruits.
Because of what is grasped, tainted phenomena arise.
When tainted phenomena are severed, that which was grasped is termed "abandonment.
It is not that there exists some separate entity called abandonment.
Treatise:
Or, because that which is "reaching" (prāpti) is the basis upon which it relies.
Commentary says:
The second master’s interpretation:
"The basis" refers to True Suchness (tathatā),
which is the basis for both delusion and awakening.
Treatise:
From the inversions of the foolish up to the realization attained through the severing of hindrances.
Commentary states:
Those who realize this suchness and attain nirvāṇa do so because nirvāṇa is itself suchness, free from all defiled phenomena;
furthermore, the conventional designation of "nirvāṇa" is established in dependence upon suchness.
The subject and its support are distinct;
this state is realized after the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) has severed the obstructions,
not within this very state itself.
Treatise:
Although in this stage one has attained what is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Commentary states:
That which is called "bodhi" is not what is intended to be revealed by the meaning of this verse.
What is intended to be revealed by the meaning of the verse is as stated in the subsequent verse: because the Dharma is named the Great Muni, the body of bliss and liberation.
"Muni" has the meaning of "tranquil silence," because it is the state of being stilled and hushed regarding all defilements.
That awakening is not merely the nature of consciousness.
Because the Great Sage is named the Dharma-body;
as stated in the Seventy-Eight [Treatises],
the two vehicles possess this name of the "liberation body" (vimukti-kāya).
Therefore, it is said that the three vehicles are equal and equal.
As for the first teacher, whose enlightenment is also termed "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
this shall be explained in its own right within the subsequent verses.
The brief explanation of these two passages is now complete.

Treatise:
"How does one realize the two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)?
The commentary states:
This asks about the cause that realizes [the result] and the result that is attained.
These two constitute the question.
The treatise states:
"This refers to that which is realized and attained within the ten stages (daśabhūmi) by means of this."
The commentary states:
This is a brief response.
Regarding "within the ten stages":
The stages traversed; the cultivation of the ten superior practices is the cause cultivated;
and the severance of the ten heavy obstructions is the dharma to be abandoned as the object of treatment.
Regarding these, they are called "heavy."
As explained at the beginning of the first fascicle, the ten true suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) are the dharmas that are the objects of contemplation;
this is due to these four kinds of causes.
The two kinds of fruits of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are realized through this.
The subsequent realization of the transformation of the basis necessarily involves sequential stages (bhūmi).
Although there are many types of stages, for now we shall speak of a small portion: the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi), which is capable of realizing [the fruit].
Therefore, at the outset, the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are first explained.
These have no separate essence;
they consist of the cultivation of ten superior practices (viśeṣacaryā).
When one cuts off the ten heavy obstructions and realizes the ten suchnesses,
it is called the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
This is a general explanation of the specific stages.
Since it is known that these stages necessarily involve spiritual practice,
the ten superior practices are explained next in relation to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to the previously mentioned non-apprehension and inconceivability, which constitute supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).
Since one practices this path, there must necessarily be its cause;
therefore, it next clarifies the severing of the ten heavy obstacles.
Thus, in the extensive verses, the abandonment of the two types of heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) is taught.
One should understand that since the ten heavy obstacles to be severed must necessarily have corresponding objects of realization,
the ten kinds of suchness (*tathatā*) are subsequently elucidated.
This refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) at the time of relinquishing the two types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), as extensively described in the verses;
although it is partially realized, it is not yet called "perfected," for this is still the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*).
This expands upon the preceding three phrases, which constitute the gradual entry [into realization]. Through this, the two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) are realized;
this clarifies the fruit that is attained.
This extensively elaborates upon the fourth line of the preceding verse to correctly clarify the process of awakening and entry;
it constitutes the second part of the brief response as a whole.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement "the ten stages," it refers to the point at which one gives rise to great joy. Commentary:
[As stated above].
The third section extensively elaborates upon the previous response;
first, it elaborates on the cause,
and subsequently, it elaborates on the result.
Within the causes, there are four parts.
First is the extensive exposition of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Within that, there are three sections.
First, the explanation of the ten distinct names;
second, the presentation of the essential nature of the stages (*bhūmi*);
third, the interpretation of the general meaning of "stages. Regarding the first point, "initially attaining the state of an ārya":
This means that when one first abandons the nature of an ordinary person and attains the nature of a noble one,
the essence of this noble nature consists of the seeds of the five aggregates that coexist with untainted,
non-conceptual wisdom and so forth.
The essence of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists solely of the seeds of the two obstacles.
If this noble nature (*āryatva*) takes up the seeds of the initial wisdom of the three vehicles, its capacity to correctly produce the manifest [wisdom] is what is termed "noble nature."
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established based on two kinds of discrimination;
even though the seeds of the two innate obstacles (*kleśa-āvaraṇa* and *jñeya-āvaraṇa*) exist,
one is not yet an ordinary person [in that sense].
Because the nature of a noble one (āryatva) is established based on the capacity to produce the initial untainted seeds,
these initial untainted seeds exist during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
yet they do not constitute the nature of a noble one at that time.
Because it has not yet arisen.
That which obstructs the noble nature by means of the obstacle of conceptualization is called the "nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).

The untainted nature (*anāsravadharmatā*) which is capable of severing the nature of an ordinary person is called the "noble nature" (*āryatva*). If this were so, then all subsequent untainted states would not be the noble nature.
This is also not the case; for it is incapable of severing the obstacle of conceptual discrimination,
and because that which was previously inferior has already been abandoned,
[this stage] possesses the capacity to sever [the obstacle].
Because it belongs to that same category,
it is also called "noble nature" (*āryatva*); yet,
as each is governed by its own respective vehicle, it remains "ordinary nature" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Furthermore, that which is capable of counteracting [the afflictions] according to one's own vehicle is termed "noble nature" (*āryatva*).
Its essence consists of the seeds of the wisdom of the single emptiness and the dual emptiness;
alternatively, its essence is the wisdom in its active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
If they were to give rise to worldly thoughts, they would not be noble ones (*ārya*).
If a Bodhisattva possesses the noble nature of a great being (*mahāsattva*), it is not like the noble nature of the "small persons" of the two vehicles;
both have realized the two kinds of emptiness.
The two vehicles and others merely realize that all is one emptiness;
now, following the conventional expression,
we say that suchness is emptiness.
It is not as if it were non-empty.
Third, it is able to benefit both self and others,
thereby distinguishing it from the two vehicles which seek only their own benefit.
Having attained the noble nature of a Mahāsattva and fully realized the two kinds of emptiness,
one gives rise to great joy because of the three causes that benefit oneself and others.
This stage is named the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This distinguishes it from subsequent stages of the bodhisattva, as the initial attainment of the noble nature (*ārya-dharma*) alone does not constitute "Supreme Joy.
Furthermore, it distinguishes it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which lack these three excellences.
At the time of first attaining the fruit, it is not called "Supreme Joy. If that is so, why is the first fruit of a bodhisattva not called "Stream-enterer"?
The Abhidharma, chapter fourteen, states:
"For what reason is it said that a bodhisattva has already attained transcendence?"
Yet they are not stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*),
because they have attained the non-abiding path (*apratiṣṭhita-mārga*) and thus do not fulfill the characteristics of a one-sided stream-enterer.
Those who have entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*) delight in abiding within the path.
Because they are weary of birth and death,
for what reason are they also not Once-returners?
Because they undergo immeasurable births within the various realms of existence.
For what reason is he also not a non-returner?
Because, while abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he returns to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: [text follows].
A Bodhisattva born in the desire realm does not fall back from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The *Abhidharma* (Thirteenth Chapter) states that Bodhisattvas are entirely free from birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration associated with dhyāna,
they are born within the desire realm or the form realm;
these are bodhisattvas who have already attained majestic power.
In all instances of taking birth,
they do so solely to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings;
for the formless realm is not a place where sentient beings can be brought to maturity.
He himself explained, saying:
"Those who dwell in meditative concentration [attain this] because of this bodhisattva’s skillful mastery of transformation."
In texts such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
there are numerous passages stating that for this reason [the practitioner] is not called a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*),
because he returns once more.
As for why they are not called *arhats*,
this may also be so named;
as was cited previously in the third fascicle.
One should know that at the end of this fascicle:
for this reason, a bodhisattva on the first ground is not called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),
and the fruit of stream-entry is not called "Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, fascicle seven, states that it is called "Joy" (*pramuditā*) solely because it possesses both types of benefit;
it is named "Supreme Joy" (*parama-pramuditā*) in contrast to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As Asvabhāva says:
If one is not endowed with joy in the first stage,
one will likewise not be endowed with it in the subsequent stages,
because this [lack] serves as the precursor.
The first fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because one initially realizes the state of sainthood through the two unsurpassed benefits, one gives rise to great joy;
thus, it is identical to these two causes."
Only this treatise uniquely teaches the realization of the two kinds of emptiness;
it is stated in [chapter] forty-seven that this stage is "well-determined."
Because of the arousal of the four marks of the mind;
because of initiating diligence and formulating correct vows;
and because of purifying and cultivating the dharmas of the stages.
Because it brings about the awakening to the remaining stages,
because it cultivates and purifies the roots of goodness,
and because it involves taking birth.
This is due to their majestic power.
This has been explained in detail in the first, second, and third fascicles of that [text] and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Although the lower fascicle of the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* provides a separate explanation of the names of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), [it is consistent with this].
Yet none compare to this;
this ground is the most supreme.
It contains ten great vows and so forth.
This is as stated in those two treatises. The treatise says:
"The second is the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (vimalā-bhūmi), because it is free from the defilements of affliction."
The commentary states:
At the time of the first bhūmi, one has already abandoned the coarse stains of transgressing the precepts;
however, it is at this second bhūmi that one is able to abandon them entirely.
This is why it is so stated;
because they are subtle compared to what precedes them,
they shall be analyzed as being subsumed within two of the eleven hindrances below.
Pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) refers to that which is associated with the prātimokṣa, the path, and meditative concentration;
thus, it encompasses all three types.
Although it is in the third bhūmi that the increase of meditative concentration first begins and one is able to abandon faults, because this [stage] has already been fulfilled,
or alternatively, it is based on the prātimokṣa.
Furthermore, it is because one is able to completely abandon the preliminary, the subsequent, and the fundamental offenses;
whereas the meditative path does not necessarily enable the abandonment of both the preliminary and subsequent offenses.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"In these two stages, one achieves natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*),
which is not like the morality of deliberate restraint (*pratisaṃkhyāna-saṃvara*) found in the first stage."
Because natural morality (prakṛti-śīla) is perfected,
all stains of transgressing the precepts have been utterly removed.
For what reason is natural morality already fully possessed by those who have attained the first fruit?
In the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it should be said that [the precepts] are not yet fully possessed;
although they are largely possessed, there still remain transgressions and subtle faults.
Furthermore, the treatise discusses the nature of natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*).
They have already been abandoned from the first bhūmi.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas who have entered the bhūmis differ from those in the first two fruits [of the śrāvaka path], as the latter still have wives and children;
yet, the Bodhisattvas never commit natural transgressions (prakṛti-sāvadya).
However, regarding prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), there may still be occasional transgressions; now, in the second bhūmi, one is able to abandon these forever.
This is consistent with other treatises.
As for the remaining points that accord with other treatises below this, I shall not trouble you with further elaboration.
The subsequent stages below are all as described in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
they are each explained in one fascicle starting from the fourth stage of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
so I shall not cite them here at length.
Treatise:
From the third stage, the Radiant, up to the Light of Sublime Wisdom. Commentary:
[As stated above].
In this stage, one achieves superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Concentration" refers to *samādhi* and *samāpatti*.
Wuxing says:
That is to say, "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) is called *samādhi* (equipoise),
while the various "ārūpyas" (formless attainments) are called *samāpatti* (attainments).
Alternatively, "samādhi" refers to...
The state of one-pointedness of mind.
As for "attainment" (samāpatti), it refers to the actualization of meditative absorption.
As previously explained,
*dhāraṇī* is here termed "total retention" (*saṃgraha*).
There are four types of total retention.
First, the Dharma;
second, the meaning;
third, the mantra.
Fourth, one is able to attain patience (*kṣānti*).
The dullness that is to be remedied on this stage constitutes an obstacle to forgetfulness regarding the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Now, this ground does not forget those dharmas;
it is called the Great Dharma Dhāraṇī.
"Dharma" refers here to the teachings.
This sublime teaching is called the Great Dharma.
With this meditative concentration and dhāraṇī as its cause,
it is able to radiate the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.
Therefore, dhāraṇī has mindfulness and wisdom as its nature;
this means that through the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—one illuminates and realizes the Mahāyāna teachings.

While these arise by way of attaining meditative concentration and severing hindrances such that hearing and reflection become increasingly superior, it is not through the power of concentration itself that these two are directly produced.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:

"It is called the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) because phenomena appear through the illumination of the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*) and so forth. Question: Why is it that meditation (*dhyāna*) is cultivated on the fifth ground among the ten perfections, and the three types of meritorious action (*puṇya-kriyā-vastu*) are cultivated?
Answer: One should understand that the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on this ground is as will be explained below.
Furthermore, these will be explained in their proper place among the eleven obstacles.
The treatise states:
"The fourth stage is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, because wisdom blazes forth."
The commentary states:
This refers specifically to the inclusion of the innate view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth within the sixth consciousness and its associates;
it does not mean all such views.
This will be understood in detail below.
Vasubandhu states:
"It is able to burn all root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) until they are reduced to ashes."
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Because the fire of wisdom burns the fuel of afflictions without forgetting them,
one takes the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as wisdom."
It is not that all [of these] are wisdom;
rather, because they are the flames of wisdom,
they are given names based on the metaphor of fire.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are as explained in a separate chapter.
The treatise states:
"The fifth is the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Ground (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), because it is extremely difficult to conquer."
The commentary states:
Vasubandhu says that the wisdom which knows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa).
One should know that the knowledge of worldly treatises and so forth is conceptual;
these two being contrary, one should practice them so as to bring them into union,
for they enable what is difficult to unite to become harmonious.
Wu-xing said:
"The wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional truths are mutually contradictory;
it is difficult to induce them so that they may be brought into mutual correspondence."
This [stage] is able to harmonize and bring about non-contradiction;
because it is superior to what preceded it,
it is called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*), not in comparison to what follows.
As for "correspondence" (saṃprayoga):
it refers to the mutual entry of the objects within true contemplation (bhūta-darśana) and conventional [contemplation] (saṃvṛti), which is called correspondence;
or it refers to the simultaneous arising of the two types of wisdom within a single moment of thought, which is called correspondence.
Now, it may also be said that they are "conjoined" (saṃyukta) because two types of wisdom arise simultaneously within a single moment;
however, this was not yet possible during the preceding four stages.
Furthermore, when the objects are identical, it is called "associated" (samprayukta).
Previously, in the first four stages, there was also a distinction between the objects of the two truths;
however, in this stage, there is no further distinction between those objects.
Because the wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional do not conflict with one another, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*).
An objection regarding this has already been raised in the second consciousness above,
as explained in detail there;
for it is known that those two objects are without distinction.
Therefore, this suchness is called "without differentiation. According to the *Śāstra*,
it is because [the bodhisattva] causes it to manifest from the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
The commentary states:
This refers to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination,

"Attention that takes all conditions as its object" refers to the attention that operates upon the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. The answer is as explained in the sixth chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
How is it that the Buddha can know common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
Since common characteristics are established based on inference (*anumāna*),

Regarding this, there are three explanations.
One interpretation holds that the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are established based on two aspects within the state of the distracted mind,
and do not refer to the concentrated mind.
If, within a concentrated mind, all objects are perceived as being subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

It is taught that the concentrated mind constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
A second interpretation states that the concentrated mind perceives only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

However, that which is induced by the skillful means of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and which takes as its object the principles manifested by those common characteristics is called "knowledge of common characteristics" from the perspective of those skillful means.

is not a common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). For this reason,

Only by contemplating the actual specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) can one sever [delusion].

Because each is attached to its own essence and is not shared with others,
if one were to establish a single category of signifier and signified through conceptual discrimination,

All states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that are free from such conceptual construction are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

Furthermore, because each individual phenomenon possesses its own distinctness, it is termed its "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because the seeds and the manifestation arise simultaneously,
the term "dysfunction" (*dausthulya*) used here does not refer to the seeds themselves; rather,
it refers to the unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) of the basis brought about by the seeds and so forth.
Although this term "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) has already been mentioned previously, it shall be understood in detail below. Question: This meaning may be so;
however, regarding each of those ten stages (*bhūmi*), stage by stage...
Since the heavy residues (dausthulya) of the afflictive obscurations are not abandoned when their seeds are severed,
they are likewise not abandoned when the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) arises.
What is it that is abandoned when the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) arises?
If, within the path of uninterrupted transition,
there is the function of abandoning the seeds of the afflictions (kleśa-bīja), [then those seeds are what is abandoned].
In the stage of the path of liberation,
one may say that the heavy impurities (*dauṣṭhulya*) are eliminated;
however, within the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), there is nothing further to be abandoned.

How is it said that the path of liberation treats the heavy residues (*dausthulya*)? Answer: Regarding the abandonment of the heavy residues of afflictions within the ten stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this does not involve the arising of a separate path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and so forth outside of the treatment for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
However, the heavy burden of the afflictions has coexisted with the cognitive obstructions since beginningless time;
the cognitive obstruction is the root.
Because the fundamental obstacles have been severed by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
the residual latencies (*dausthulya*) of both the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) [are eliminated].
Since it is abandoned within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*),
this fault does not arise; therefore,
the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of these afflictions is not capable of causing rebirth.
It merely obstructs the stages;
therefore, it is abandoned simultaneously with the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) and not left behind.
Thus, there is no such fault as there is in the case of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth.

This will be understood below. Question: If that is so, then as with those of the two vehicles who only sever the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and do not sever the seeds [of the cognitive obstacles], there would be no "heaviness" (*dausthulya*) at the stage when the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) arises.
What is the purpose of further arising the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? Answer:

It is because one eliminates the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) without interruption and attains mastery within the path of liberation. Question: Once the coarse heaviness has been severed, does one attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 360, states that Subhūti asked:
If unconditioned phenomena were without distinction,
why did the Buddha say that the continuity of habitual tendencies (vāsanā-saṃtati) is forever absent in the Tathāgata?
The two vehicles still possess them.
The World-Honored One replied:
"The continuity of habitual tendencies is truly not affliction."
Within the bodies of those of the two vehicles, that which induces what is meaningless cannot be drawn forth;
within the body of a bodhisattva, that which induces what is meaningless can be drawn forth;
in a Tathāgata, it is forever absent.
Precisely by this passage,
it is shown that the severance of habitual tendencies does not result in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Otherwise, there would have to be distinctions among the unconditioned.

This also demonstrates that the abandonment of the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) does not result in the attainment of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). If the abandonment of the cognitive obstacles were to result in the attainment of the unconditioned,
it would then follow that the three vehicles (triyāna) also attain the unconditioned, yet there would still be distinctions between them.
Fifth, these obscurations consist of twenty-two delusions (*moha*).
The treatise states:
although [these are] within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they reach the level of the fundamental [delusions].
The commentary states:
This reveals that the obstructions of ordinary beings do not exhaustively encompass all phenomena,
because karma and so forth are not mentioned here as fundamental [obstructions].
The term "and so forth" includes non-karmic and non-retributive states in the miserable destinies,
as well as other phenomena such as dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*),
and the various types of karma produced within the human and celestial destinies.
Furthermore, because it includes both the cause and the fruit,
and because stating that they are subsumed under the miserable destinies (*durgati*) alone would be incomplete,
only the afflictions (*kleśa*) are mentioned among those capable of giving rise [to rebirth].
Because the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) coexist with them, they are collectively termed "afflictions" (kleśa). According to the treatise, by virtue of this,
from the first stage (bhūmi) onward, [one perceives] all karmic fruits and so forth.
The commentary states:
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter seventy-eight, and other texts explain the abandonment of two types of ignorance;
this may be understood according to the text. Regarding "the various karmas, fruits, and so forth":
The preceding term "and so forth" (ādi) sequentially includes the distinct karmas arising from discrimination within the happy realms,
as well as their results and so on.
To speak directly of the miserable realms (*apāya*) alone would not encompass them all;
for since the Sūtra speaks of the defilements of the miserable realms, [it must include other factors as well].
The term "affliction" (*saṃkleśa*) applies generally to the afflictions of the higher realms (*sugati*), because it encompasses their conceptual proliferation.
While it was previously stated that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is abandoned through the severance of its objects and fetters and is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*),
what is said here is that its fruit is abandoned through non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This is the second interpretation, as it is stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Why is karmic fruit also called "delusion"?
Treatise:
It should be understood that the section on the category of delusion (*moha-pakṣa*) is explained hereafter by analogy with this.
Commentary states:
Although the essence of various karmas and their fruits is not delusion itself,
karma arises from delusion and its fruits are brought about by delusion.
Because it is the category of the foolish,
it is also called "foolishness.
Subsequent mentions of "foolishness" in the various stages (*bhūmi*) should be understood according to this explanation.
Just as there is delusion regarding karma and its destinations in the second bhūmi,
it is not because their essential nature is delusion.
Furthermore, within the obstacles of initial attachment to self and phenomena:
Furthermore, there are also instances where greed, views, and so forth are not themselves delusion (*moha*),
yet they belong to the category of delusion;
the following cases should be understood accordingly.
However, although the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) exists within the obscuration of conceptualization,
it does not incite karma that brings about birth and death,
because it is not a binding phenomenon (bandhana-dharma).
Now, regarding this first category of karmic results produced,
the term "destinations" (*gati*) is used here as a term of disparagement.
As it is said, "The *paṇḍaka* is called a miserable destination (*apāya*) among humans. According to the treatise,
this may refer only to the two types of delusion that arise simultaneously with [the afflictions].
The commentary states:
The term "first" refers to attachment;
it clarifies that this is the delusion arising simultaneously with the category of obstacles to benefit (*hita-vibandha*).
The second refers to the affliction of the miserable realms (*apāya-saṃkleśa*);
it is not necessarily the fruit of karma,
but rather the delusion that arises concomitantly with the category of dull obstacles (*mṛdv-āvaraṇa-pakṣa*).
"Reproach" refers to the destinies (*gati*).
Within this context, other afflictions are not mentioned separately;
these other afflictions merely belong to the categories of sharp or dull hindrances.
The delusion that arises simultaneously is simply ignorance (*avidyā*).
According to this master’s intention,
it is taught that only when ignorance is associated with views or non-views is it designated as "sharp" or "dull."
This is because it is taught that within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the ten types of ignorance (*avidyā*) are severed;
therefore, other afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are not included.
[Treatise]
Regarding the statement that "those *dausthulyas* [refer to] the state of being unamenable," the commentary says:
"Those words refer to *dausthulya*."
What is "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*)?
It is revealed to be the seeds of those two delusions;
the former two [delusions] are active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Because the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) are the seeds. Question: Since the manifest activities have long since ceased, how can one say they are "abandoned"?
Answer: The fifty-ninth [chapter] states that there are, in brief, two kinds of abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
First, the abandonment of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*);
second, the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Therefore, it is said that both types of manifestation are abandoned. Question: Why is this not a case of abandoning the manifestation through the suppression (*vibhava*) of its activity? Answer: It is not so.
In the subsequent text of that fascicle, the two terms "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) are explained.
Regarding "the abandonment of the envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*),
this refers to the abandonment of greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).
Up to the abandonment of doubt and the five views;
this is the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering,
up to the abandonment of that which is bound to the formless realm.
The severance of the fetters is the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Since one does not suppress the afflictions of the path of seeing at the time of suppressing the [other] afflictions,
it is known that these two delusions are active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) is the seed.
Furthermore, it is explained that,
according to your own intention, the former two are the seeds.
Dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) is not a seed;
rather, it is the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) arising from these two categories.
Its stage of abandonment is explained in the same manner as that of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and others.
Treatise:
As with entering the second dhyāna, this should be explained by analogy.
Commentary says:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states:
"In the second dhyāna, the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned.
The seeds of the faculty of suffering were already abandoned in the first dhyāna."
Now, the heavy impurities (*dausthulya*) of that root of suffering are severed;
this is because it is taught that the second dhyāna severs that root of suffering.
The heavy impurities of the subsequent stages should be understood accordingly as two interpretations.
The sixth [point] concerns whether the obscuration that is ignorance is the same as or different [from the other obscurations].
The treatise states:
"Although [ignorance] is abandoned in the first bhūmi, it extends through the ten categories of delusion."
The commentary states:
The intended meaning here is that,
in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one truly abandons the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).
Now, in explaining the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*),
we take only the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and not the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
according to the seventh fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*.
The ten kinds of ignorance are said to be non-defiled when considered in relation to the two vehicles;
however, if one takes them as afflictions (*kleśa*), these ten ignorances are all defiled.
This is because ignorance is precisely the delusion (*moha*) within the category of the ten hindrances, and delusion is itself ignorance.
For what reason does the treatise not state that the ignorance of the first bhūmi is admitted to be defiled and a seed of both obstructions?
[The answer is:
Even the followers of the two vehicles are able to reach this state; it is simply not what is being discussed here.
The commentary states:
Those of the two vehicles are also able to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
for the severance of the afflictive hindrances is common [to them].
This is not what is being discussed here.
Those of the two vehicles cannot abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
the cognitive obstruction is unique [to Bodhisattvas].
Therefore, regarding the ignorance of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*),
it is said only that it is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
As the *Vasubandhu-ṭīkā* (She lun) states:
Furthermore, because there are ten obstacles to be remedied, the ten stages (bhūmis) are established as distinct.
The treatise further states that the ten types of ignorance extend to those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The commentary states:
Regarding the description as "non-defiled," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Original Text) says:
Regarding the ten types of non-defiled ignorance within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
these are explained solely in reference to what is abandoned through cultivation on the ten stages (bhūmi);
they are not said to be the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva), because that is abandoned through insight (darśana-prahātavya).
How is this known? The *Abhidharmapada* (Dharma-pāda), chapter fourteen, states:
"Having already attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*)."
Within that stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
one cultivates only the paths that serve as antidotes to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); therefore,
those [afflictions] abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are not included in the enumeration of the ten types of ignorance.
Because it is taught that [the state of being an ordinary person] is not defiled;
if the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were itself defiled,
then by this [teaching] one would know [otherwise].
That state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is not non-defiled.
Vasubandhu further states:
"The ten stages (bhūmi) are established separately in order to counteract the ten types of ignorance."
Since the ten types of ignorance are explained as being distinct from the ten obstacles,
the ten ignorances are not identical to the ten obstacles;
for that [text] itself provides two successive expositions of the ten ignorances.
However, regarding the absence of intrinsic nature, there is only one interpretation, and it is not explained separately.
[The opponent] asks: "Does the cultivation of the path in the ten stages also suppress the afflictions?"
Regarding the severance of the heavy impediments (*dausthulya*) of those afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*):
why is it that [the text] does not speak of them as "the two obstructions and the faults of the three bases," as previously stated?
Treatise:
Although this stage is reached within this state, it is not mentioned here.
Commentary says:
Within the stage of the path of cultivation of the ten bhūmis,
one likewise suppresses the afflictions and eliminates their coarse residues (dausthulya),
yet this is not the primary intention.
Why is this so? Because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not abandoned, this is not mentioned here.
This is stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and by Vasubandhu and others.
Because Bodhisattvas on the ten stages intentionally retain the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to assist their vows for rebirth, this is not their primary intent;
rather, their intention is directed toward wisdom, which aims at the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
and thus they sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is the non-interruption of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions.
Question: If that is so, why is it that only the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is mentioned in the first stage (*bhūmi*)?
It does not state that the obstacles to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are further severed.
According to the treatise, in reality, this should be understood as applying from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onwards.
The commentary states:
The Master of the Treatise replies:
Although it is true that one has already emerged from the Path of Vision at the first stage (*bhūmi*),...
Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one also abandons a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Since we are currently speaking from the beginning among the ten obstacles, the obstacles of cultivation are not mentioned;
as the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) is already discussed from the outset.
The nine obstacles described in the subsequent nine stages should be understood accordingly as all being derived from what was stated at the outset.

How is this known? It is because one has already abandoned the remaining afflictions after entering the mind of the stage, emerging from the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and so forth, in the first stage and the others.
Treatise:
When abiding in the stage of fulfillment, the Path should have no distinctions.
Commentary says:
Now, I shall answer according to principle:
the time spent dwelling in the stages of fulfillment (bhūmi) is already protracted,
namely two asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
This principle should further be refuted.
If it were not further refuted in this way,
then since the paths of the three times within the stages would lack their three grades, [the system would be untenable].
Because there should be no distinction. The treatise states:
"Therefore it is said that when a bodhisattva reaches [the final stage], they abandon [the afflictions] all at once."
The commentary states:
Citing fourteen passages from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as proof,
it is shown that if one abides in the mind of a perfected stage (*pūrṇabhūmi-citta*), one no longer further abandons afflictions (*kleśa*).
How do the treatises explain the cultivation of the path across the ten stages?

Specifically, they state that within the first stage (*bhūmi*), one only abandons the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) and does not further abandon the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*).
Because there are nine stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The afflictions are suppressed but not extinguished."
Like poison neutralized by a mantra,
one retains the afflictions until they are exhausted,
thereby realizing the Buddha’s omniscience.
Vasubandhu states:
Because they retain the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of afflictions,
they do not proceed as swiftly toward parinirvāṇa as the followers of the two vehicles.
Therefore, they retain their afflictions to assist their vows for rebirth and so forth;
that is to say, because all bodhisattvas, through the power of great compassion,
aspire toward omniscience.
The intention is directed toward the path that counteracts the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
rather than the path that counteracts the afflictions (*kleśa*),
because one intends to take birth within saṃsāra out of compassion and the vow to assist others.
It is called "retaining afflictions.
Otherwise, the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata would be at its most extreme;
he should have retained afflictions in order to manifest birth according to the various classes of beings.
From this it is known that because the mind does not incline toward cessation, it is termed "retained";
it is only when one is about to attain Buddhahood that it is suddenly and completely severed.
These are the fourteen passages from the Abhidharma. The treatise states:
"The second is the obstacle of wrong conduct, which leads to the transgression of the three types of action."
The commentary states:
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says that wrong conduct constitutes an obstruction to the bodies and so forth of sentient beings.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of Vasubandhu states:
"Regarding the obstacles of improper conduct toward the bodies and so forth of sentient beings,
the meaning is essentially the same."
The term "obscuration to the knowable" (jñeyāvaraṇa) distinguishes it from the obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).
The expression "innate" (sahaja) distinguishes it from that which arises through conceptual construction (vikalpita).
The description of it as being "a portion" distinguishes it from other obscurations to the knowable that are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The following is explained according to this interpretation: those who commit transgressions through the three karmas are called "fools" because they belong to the category of the foolish.
The explanation is as before. Question: Regarding the two aforementioned types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), [which one...]
It is said that the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) cannot incite karma.

Why, then, is it stated here that the three types of karma incited by a portion of the innate [obstruction] constitute "delusion regarding karma and its destinations" (*karmagatimoha*)? (See *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, fascicle 7).

It is also said that whatever karma is produced and whatever fruit is obtained are both the substance of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Answer: If it were to produce karma and bring about birth and death, the cognitive hindrance would simply be incapable of doing so.
Because they are not bound by dharmas,
the first two types of birth and death are said not to arise on this account;
if they obstruct wisdom, the three karmas do not bring about evil fruits.
This can also give rise [to it].

What is clarified in this passage is merely the result of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and dominant (*adhipati*) karma. Question: Since attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) extends to the unwholesome (*akuśala*), why is it not a bond (*bandhana*)?
Answer: It is not by virtue of its unwholesome nature alone that something constitutes a bond.

Just as the nature of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and so forth is not bondage, so too the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is rendered unwholesome only because it is concomitant with afflictions;
its intrinsic nature is not bondage. If this is so, why does it not induce maturation (*vipāka*)? As for the actual meaning:
Although it is associated with an unwholesome mind, it is still termed neutral (*avyākṛta*).
This is because the perspectives of Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles differ;
specifically, it is categorized as both obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Since it cannot produce results such as maturation (*vipāka-phala*),
the aforementioned objection does not apply.
Treatise.
"Those obstacles range from the second bhūmi up to the transgressions of the three types of karma.
Commentary states:
Because these karmas can obstruct the pure śīla (ethical discipline) of the second bhūmi.
The term "destiny" (gati) refers to being subject to censure and reproach,
as in the case of the evil destinies (durgati).
It cannot be said that what takes up a destiny is itself the destiny.
Because one does not take up evil fruits, the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) is as previously described;
therefore, it is not explained separately.
As for the mention of "body" and so forth in other treatises:
This refers to the three types of action (trikarma),
as these words already encompass all forms of misconduct.
Treatise.
"Or there is only the delusion regarding the undertaking of karma, but not the delusion regarding the completion of karma. Commentary:
This is the second interpretation.
The former is the delusion that initiates karma;
the latter is the delusion of not understanding karma, which is not itself the karma being initiated.
Furthermore, this [latter] is not necessarily capable of initiating karma.
Because the objects and functions differ. The treatise states:
"The third is the obstacle of dullness, which extends to the forgetting of the dharma during cultivation."
The commentary states:
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says that the characteristic of darkness is the obscuration of forgetfulness regarding the various dharmas of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:
"Second, those of dull faculties experience forgetfulness regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
(Treatise)
Those obstacles to the third stage can be permanently severed once [the practitioner] attains it.
The commentary states:
"Superior concentration" refers to...
This refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
It encompasses all the dhyānas, formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
Regarding "retention" (*dhāraṇī*), it is explained as comprising forty-five types, including those of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
It takes mindfulness and wisdom as its essence.
As stated in the Forty-Five [Discourses],
there are four dhāraṇīs.
The dharmas, meanings, and mantras enable one to attain the bodhisattva's patiences;
these are now subsumed under the first two [categories],
namely, the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
Furthermore, there are the three types of wisdom (prajñā) produced by meditative concentration (samādhi) and so forth:
meditative wisdom (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) is directly produced by concentration,
while the wisdoms of hearing (śrutamayī) and reflection (cintāmayī) are directly produced by the dhāraṇīs.
Therefore, these are combined into a single textual unit along with the three sublime types of wisdom (prajñā) they produce.
These three types of wisdom have wisdom as their essential nature;
it is said that one cultivates wisdom by practicing its causes, thereby attaining this wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that one "cultivates wisdom";
this is named after its cause,
for cultivation itself is not wisdom.
Because one cultivates this concentration. The treatise states:
"By means of this, from the third stage up to the cultivation of wisdom."
The commentary states:
For those who desire and are deluded regarding the obstruction of superior meditative concentration and the cultivation of wisdom,
it is precisely because they give rise to craving for the five objects of desire that they dwell frequently in distraction.
It obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Since the cultivation of wisdom is closely associated with concentration, only these two are mentioned as being obstructed; however, this does not mean that it does not also obstruct reflection (*cintā*) and other forms of wisdom.
Question: "Desire and greed" (*kāmarāga*) is a term for an affliction (*kleśa*).
For what reason is it called "desire and greed" (*chandarāga*) among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
The treatise states:
Because in the past, for the most part, they were associated with and operated in dependence upon that [desire and greed].
The commentary states:

Regarding that cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), this third delusion is frequently associated with sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) among the afflictions; therefore, it is called the "delusion of sensual desire."
The entity of the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is not what is termed desire-attachment (kāmarāga).
Since that [desire-attachment] obstructs meditative concentration (samādhi) and the wisdom of cultivation, it is said that when the cognitive obscuration is permanently severed,
desire-attachment is thereby subdued.
Because the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are fundamentally severed,
the afflictions (*kleśa*), which are merely their branches, are thereby subdued.
This is because these afflictions have operated in dependence upon the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) since beginningless time.
Treatise:
Regarding the second [point], "the perfection of hearing and retention up to the wisdom of hearing and reflection," the commentary states:
Because hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) are closely related to hearing and retention (*dhāraṇī*), they are mentioned specifically;
it is not that they do not obstruct the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī prajñā*).
Nevertheless, because they constitute the most prominent obstacles, they are distinguished as two separate categories.
Although the two obstacles are explained as distinct in terms of their nature and meaning, they are not one;
this refers to the delusions of the three stages above,
which differ from the seventy-eight [delusions] and so forth.
Treatise:
Regarding the "hindrance of the manifestation of subtle afflictions," it is described as "subtle" up to that point.
Commentary: [As follows].
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* speaks of the "obstruction of pride regarding the understanding of dharmas";
this is a difference in terminology used by the translators,
referring precisely to the pride of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
